newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Thai devaluation gives Brazil "wake-up call".
newsitem.headline: Thai devaluation gives Brazil "wake-up call".

text.p: Thailand's move to float its over-valued baht currency, which resulted in a 15-20 percent devaluation, should serve as a warning to Brazil, whose external accounts are steadily deteriorating, economists said.
"What happened in Thailand was a wake-up call for Brazil to look more carefully at its external accounts," said Marcelo Carvalho, J.P. Morgan's chief Brazil economist.
"We don't see a crisis in the short-term, but we cannot have a large widening in the current account gap," Carvalho said.
Brazil, with its strong currency, high interest rates and mounting trade deficit, has often been compared with Thailand over the past year.
While Brazil's fundamentals are stronger, backed in part by close to $60 billion in foreign reserves, the country could learn from Thailand's experience, economists said.

They note that the root cause of devaluations in emerging market countries, like Mexico's 1994 peso crisis or Thailand's devaluation earlier this week, has been an inability to finance the current account balance of payments gaps that strong currencies generate.

Both Mexico and Thailand had current account shortfalls in the range of seven to eight percent of gross domestic product. Brazil's current account gap is in substantially better shape, at about four percent of GDP. But the trend is deteriorating.

For one, Brazil's trade deficit, the leading cause of its current account woes, is expected to hit a whopping $13 billion this year, more than twice the size of last year's $5.5 billion gap. Continued heavy trade imbalances are forecast to push Brazil's current account gap over 5.0 percent of GDP in 1998.
At the heart of Brazil's poor trade picture, economists say, is its strong currency, the real, which this week completed its third anniversary.
Although the strong real has helped slash annual inflation from close to 3,000 percent in July 1994 to about eight percent today, it has led to record trade gaps.

Few Brazil watchers expect the government to devalue the real prior to October 1998 presidential elections. But many economists are beginning to think the Central Bank will be forced to do something by early 1999.

The most likely scenario, they say, would be to speed depreciation of the real against the dollar -- now at about seven percent a year -- to about 15-20 percent, at least in the first year of the next administration.
Brazilian officials, however, say they are adamant about leaving things they way they are and say speculation about devaluation and comparisons with Thailand are unfair.

"The consequences for Brazil are nil... These are two countries that are distant in terms of geography and their economies," Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola said Thursday responding to questions about Thailand.
The Brazilian government says it is healthy for developing nations to run large trade and current account gaps, which reflect greater opening and a modernization of local industry.

Another point the government tries to hammer home is the fact that foreign direct investment in Brazil, which is expected to reach $15 billion this year, finances up to 40 percent of the current account shortfall.

"This was not the case in Thailand," said one economist who asked not to be named. "I think it is obvious to say the Thai situation should put Brazil on the alert, but I don't think it is fair to draw closer comparisons," he said.
